title: Optical Interference for the Guidance of Cryogenic Focused Ion Beam Milling Beyond the Axial Diffraction Limit
content: Cryogenic electron tomography (Cryo-ET) has been utilized as a powerful approach to observe the subcellular architecture and even molecular scale structures in situ.[1-3] However, it is limited to samples or regions of samples far thinner than typical cells, ∼300 nm. [4] Cryogenic focused-ion-beam milling (Cryo-FIB), which utilizes an ion beam to ablate cellular material, has been developed to cut thin subsections of a cell to a desirable thickness. Cryo-FIB milling is a destructive approach with only the final thin section being preserved for high-resolution Cryo-ET imaging, thus targeting of FIB milling process is of prime importance. Targeting via fluorescence microscopy is a promising route with latest Cryo-FIB systems often incorporating a light microscope into the vacuum chamber. However, these integrated systems often position the focus of the light microscope and Cryo-FIB in two different locations. This geometry necessitates that the two modalities first be registered computationally to guide the milling process, a workflow fraught with experimental errors and uncertainties. [5-7] We amend this by utilizing a tri-coincident system that allows simultaneous fluorescence microscopy and Cryo-FIB milling. [8] Here, I will discuss our ability to direct milling in two distinct ways depending on the axial extent of the target structure. Neither approach requires the addition of fiducials, or registration, but can guide the milling process with precision more than an order of magnitude beyond the axial diffraction limit. Lastly, I will highlight each approach on a distinct biological structure in situ.
